questions.question: A grid has 20 equal unit squares (4 rows of 5). Each little square has sides 1 unit long. Exactly 12 of those squares are shaded, and they form a rectangle 4 units wide and 3 units tall. Perimeter means the distance all the way around the outside of the shaded shape. What is its perimeter?
questions.explain: Perimeter counts the unit edges along the outside: 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 units. The usual trap is answering 12 because 12 squares are shaded — squares inside measure how much space, edges outside measure the distance around.

questions.question: A grid has 24 equal unit squares (4 rows of 6), and each square has sides 1 unit long. Exactly 12 squares are shaded and they make a rectangle 6 units wide and 2 units tall. What is the perimeter of the shaded rectangle?
questions.explain: Walk around the outside and count unit edges: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 units. Watch two traps — saying 12 because 12 squares are shaded, and stopping after only three sides.

questions.question: A grid has 15 equal unit squares (3 rows of 5). Each square has sides 1 unit long. Exactly 5 squares are shaded, all in one row, making a long strip 5 units wide and 1 unit tall. What is the perimeter of the strip?
questions.explain: Go around the outside: 5 units along the top, 1 down the end, 5 back along the bottom, 1 up the other end, so 5 + 1 + 5 + 1 = 12 units. Answering 5 counts the shaded squares instead of the edges, and answering 10 forgets the two short ends.

questions.question: A grid has 21 equal unit squares (3 rows of 7), each square 1 unit on every side. Exactly 14 squares are shaded and they form a rectangle 7 units wide and 2 units tall. What is the perimeter of that shaded rectangle?
questions.explain: Add the unit edges around the outside: 7 + 2 + 7 + 2 = 18 units. The 14 is the number of shaded squares, not the distance around — the squares fill the shape, the edges fence it.

questions.question: A polygon is drawn on grid paper so that every side follows the grid lines. What should you count to find its perimeter?
options: Count the unit edges along the outside of the shape
Count how many squares are in the longest row
Count the shaded squares inside the shape
Count the corners of the shape
questions.explain: Perimeter is the distance around, so you count the unit edges you travel along the outside border. Counting the squares inside tells you how much space is covered, which is a different measurement.

questions.question: On a geoboard, Priya stretches an elastic band into a rectangle that is 7 units long and 4 units wide. What is the perimeter of her rectangle?
questions.explain: Count the unit edges all the way around: 7 + 4 + 7 + 4 = 22 units. The 28 comes from counting the little squares the band encloses, and 11 comes from adding the length and width only once instead of twice.

questions.question: On grid paper, Ethan colours a rectangle 2 squares tall and 6 squares wide. Ava colours a rectangle 3 squares tall and 4 squares wide. Both used 12 squares. Whose rectangle has the greater perimeter?
options: They are equal, because both are made of 12 squares
They are equal, because both shapes are rectangles
questions.explain: Count edges around each one: 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 16 units, while 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14 units, so the long thin one has the greater perimeter. Shapes made from the same number of squares can still have different perimeters — the squares inside do not decide the distance around.

questions.question: A rectangle drawn on grid paper is 8 units long and 5 units wide, with each side following the grid lines. What is its perimeter?
questions.explain: Add all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 units. The 40 counts the unit squares covered rather than the edges around the outside, and 21 misses one of the sides.

questions.question: Sofia sketches her rectangular vegetable patch on grid paper: 6 units long and 4 units wide, where 1 unit stands for 1 metre. She wants fencing all the way around, and fencing costs $3 per metre. How much will the fencing cost?
questions.explain: First find the perimeter by counting edges around: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 m, then 20 x $3 = $60. The $72 comes from using the 24 squares inside the patch instead of the distance around it — fencing follows the border, not the ground inside.

questions.question: Liam draws a square on grid paper that is 4 units on every side. He counts the 16 unit squares inside it and says the perimeter is 16 units. His number happens to be correct. What is wrong with his thinking?
options: His method works for every shape, because the number of squares inside is always the perimeter
He counted squares, not the unit edges around the outside; a 4 by 4 square just happens to have 16 outside edges too
He should have counted the 4 corners instead
Counting squares always works for squares, so his method is fine here
questions.explain: Perimeter means the unit edges around the border: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 units, which for a 4 by 4 square is a coincidence with its 16 inside squares. Test his method on a 2 by 6 rectangle — 12 squares inside but a perimeter of 16 units — and it falls apart.

questions.question: A schoolyard planter is drawn on grid paper as a plus sign: one unit square in the middle, with one unit square touching each of its four sides (top, bottom, left and right), so 5 squares are shaded. Each unit edge on the grid stands for 2 metres. The class wants a low wooden border all the way around the planter. How many metres of border do they need?
questions.explain: Trace the outside of the plus: each of the 4 arm squares shows 3 outside edges, so 4 x 3 = 12 unit edges, and 12 x 2 m = 24 m. The 10 m comes from counting the 5 shaded squares instead of the edges, and 12 m forgets that each unit edge is worth 2 metres.

questions.question: A garden club in Abbotsford draws a U-shaped flower bed on grid paper: a bottom row of 3 unit squares, with 1 more square sitting on top of the left end square and 1 more on top of the right end square, so 5 squares are shaded and there is a dip in the middle of the top. Each unit edge stands for 1 metre. Plastic edging costs $4 per metre and must run all the way around the bed, including down into the dip. How much will the edging cost?
questions.explain: Trace every outside edge, dipping into the U: that is 12 unit edges, so 12 m, and 12 × $4 = $48. The $20 comes from counting the 5 shaded squares instead of the edges, $40 goes straight across the top and skips the dip (only 10 m), and $12 is the metres of edging before the price is applied.
